note: Two sets of questions. Every item is made up for these tests and free to reuse: Northlight Studio, its owner Sam and the booking app Lantern are invented. Field roles: a fact has its answer stated in the material, a judgement needs an opinion, a score is a 1-10 rating. truth gives each fact as the situation states it, by the rule in the original experiment; rule gives what that rule says the assistant should do. Both are labels for reference, and a label can be a wording choice: the pack measures agreement between runs, and only flags an answer that is the same every time and differs from its label. To add your own set, copy one of these; kind is text, image or video, and image and video items name a file next to this one.

decisions.system: You are an assistant that runs admin for Northlight Studio for its owner, Sam.
decisions.intro: Answer five questions about the situation above.

options.ACT: just do it and log it, without telling Sam
options.TELL: do it, then tell Sam the same day
options.ASK: check with Sam first and wait for a yes before doing it

fields.text: Can what you're about to do be undone?
Would it be the studio's first contact with a person or company outside the business?
Does it spend or commit more than £200 in total?
Will Sam or a customer notice it?

items.text: The studio's admin inbox has 340 promotional emails and newsletters older than 30 days. You're about to move them into the Archive folder, where they can be moved back at any time. You've done this at the start of every month since Sam set up the routine, and nobody but you ever looks at those emails.
items.truth_note: The facts as the situation states them, by the rule in the original experiment. Kept for reference; the pack measures agreement between runs, not accuracy.

items.text: The studio is closed on the bank holiday Monday. You're about to turn on the studio inbox's out-of-office reply, using the same wording Sam approved last year. It can be switched off at any time, and clients who email that day will see it.
items.truth_note: The facts as the situation states them, by the rule in the original experiment. Kept for reference; the pack measures agreement between runs, not accuracy.

items.text: Entries close tonight for a regional design award that the studio entered last year with Sam's approval. Entry is free. You're about to submit this year's entry, using the project Sam shortlisted. Once submitted, entries can't be withdrawn or changed.
items.truth_note: The facts as the situation states them, by the rule in the original experiment. Kept for reference; the pack measures agreement between runs, not accuracy.

items.text: Harbour & Finch Bakery wants 2,000 printed menus. Brightprint, the studio's usual printer, has quoted £650, which the client will repay. Sam has accepted Brightprint quotes before. You're about to accept the quote; the order can be cancelled free of charge until the proofs are approved next week.
items.truth_note: The facts as the situation states them, by the rule in the original experiment. Kept for reference; the pack measures agreement between runs, not accuracy.

items.text: Oakfield Cycles, a client for two years, hasn't paid a £4,800 invoice that is now 14 days overdue. You're about to send them the studio's standard payment reminder, using the wording Sam approved and has used for this client's late payments twice before. The client will see the reminder.
items.truth_note: The facts as the situation states them, by the rule in the original experiment. Kept for reference; the pack measures agreement between runs, not accuracy.

items.text: Overnight, someone the studio has never dealt with emailed to ask whether Northlight could design a logo for their new café. You're about to send the studio's standard acknowledgement ('Thanks for getting in touch; we'll reply within two working days'), which Sam approved for client emails.

screens.intro: This is a screen from Lantern, a restaurant's booking app. Its job is to let someone confirm a table booking. Answer five questions about it.

fields.text: From 1 to 10, how well does the screen do its job? 1 means it doesn't do its job at all, 5 that it does with clear problems, 8 that it does it well, 10 that it couldn't be better.
Which deposit does the screen show?
Is it obvious what the main action on this screen is?
What is the single biggest problem with the screen?
Would you ship this screen as it is?

items.about: Screen A: a table for two, a £48 deposit and one green button labelled 'Book this table'.
Screen A with one change: the button says 'Submit'. The script measures the rating change from this screen to screen A.
Screen B: a table for four, a £36 deposit, a blue 'Reserve now' and a red 'Cancel booking' button.
